chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Hisham and Hafs ibn al-Bakhtari, from the one who mentioned him, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) — regarding
the man who marries in temporary marriage (mut'a) — does it make him muhsan (married)? He said: No. That is only applicable to the permanent thing with him.

key_terms.الشَّيْءِ الدَّائِمِ: The permanent thing — a reference to the permanent, ongoing marital relationship (nikah da'im) as opposed to the fixed-term mut'a contract
key_terms.الْمُتْعَةَ: Mut'a — temporary marriage with a fixed duration, recognized in Shia jurisprudence as lawful based on Quran 4:24
key_terms.تُحْصِنُهُ: From ihsan/tahsin — the legal state of being 'married' (muhsan), which in classical Islamic penal law is the condition that escalates the punishment for adultery (zina) to stoning (rajm)

ai.seo_question: Does temporary marriage (mut'a) make a man muhsan in Shia Islam?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) was asked whether contracting a temporary marriage (mut'a) grants a man the legal status of being 'married' (muhsan/ihsan), which in Islamic penal law is the prerequisite for the hadd punishment of stoning (rajm) if the person commits adultery. The Imam categorically answered no — the status of ihsan that triggers the capital punishment applies only to a man who has a permanent wife living with him. This ruling reflects the classical Shia jurisprudential distinction between the permanent marriage (nikah da'im) and temporary marriage (nikah al-mut'a or nikah al-inqita'), with far-reaching implications for penal law.
